name: Yusuf Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI firms, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. What do you do on a normal factory day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a robot welding cell for farm-trailer frames. The arm lays the long seams; I clamp steel in a jig, check the bead, and mend awkward corners by hand. I have a vocational certificate and know the settings well enough to spot a bad clamp before the robot runs. I enjoy the first clean seam on a new trailer model.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What else matters around that shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Hana and I have two children in school and a mortgage. My welding-cell pay is good, and we have about nine months of expenses saved; Hana works, but I budget the house on my known wage rather than guessing what she might earn next month. I use AI every day for manuals and setup notes, then test every suggestion safely. On weekends I print replacement plastic clips for old motorbikes and sell a few online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the welders AI remains a decent manual search, not a magic torch. The jig still has to hold the frame square before the robot starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cell needs an operator and my wage looks sound if AI stays modest. Nine months saved lets us absorb a quiet spell, and there are other factories nearby. I would still like a better tool for finding a faulty seam, but I do not need it to pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the welding cell, checking the seams and selling printed motorbike clips on weekends. If spring orders cover the printer’s parts and postage, I would buy a second printer from those profits to fill more paid orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work and the mortgage. A slower technology story would be a little dull, but a sound weld is enough excitement on some mornings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the new printer have paying work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would order it only after I have enough spring clip orders to keep the first printer busy for several weekends. A spare machine on a shelf earns nothing. I can show Hana the actual invoices before buying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the AI assistant make you faster on the cell already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me find a manual page, but I still check the fixture and the weld test myself. I cannot send a trailer frame out because a chat box called it sound. The cell log has measured results for that reason.

say: I would **tell** welders AI search helps with manuals while the jig and weld still need checks.
I would **not** confuse faster notes with a tested trailer frame.
think: My **welding-cell** wage is secure and nine months saved covers ordinary gaps.
A **second** printer is attractive only if paying clip orders justify it.
do: **Keep** setting the welding cell and checking trailer-frame seams.
**Continue** selling printed motorbike clips on weekends.
**Buy** a second printer only from profit after enough paid orders cover its use.
feel: **Calm** about wages, with a little boredom if AI stops improving.
S0.quote: A spare machine on a shelf earns nothing.
fieldNote: **Yusuf** already runs a robot cell and uses AI daily, but tests physical welds and fixtures himself.
His **strong** reserve and higher pay make the plateau safe; a second printer is a conditional business purchase.
The **purchase** depends on actual paid clip orders and profit, not an assumed household income from Hana.

steps.text: Keep setting the welding cell and testing trailer-frame seams
Continue selling printed motorbike clips on weekends
Buy second printer from profit only after paid clip orders justify it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shop that planning software may pick weld paths before a robot can load an odd trailer frame. I would ask for paid training before the manager expects one operator to cover two cells.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could probably run a newer cell, since I already handle one, but a program that writes its own path makes my setup skill less rare. I do not think my whole wage disappears in this milder picture, yet the roster could tighten. I also think of the hand welders on short runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new AI weld-path checker on scrap test pieces if the plant approves it and a supervisor signs off the safety procedure. I would request a paid supplier course for two-cell operation and take it if offered with a supervised place and written hours and wage at least matching mine. I would keep the current cell and clip sales while the roster is decided.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible cut in my own hours. I am keen to learn, but the written pay line matters more than being first to touch a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you share the setup notes with hand welders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I would show them the safe test routine and what the checker gets wrong. A written guide can help the night shift too. But I would not promise them two cells create two new jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the supplier course is not offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the present cell and check posted welding-cell roles at nearby plants. I would apply only if the wage and shift cover our mortgage and school pickup. I would not leave a good wage for a trial I have merely requested.

say: I would **ask** for paid training before one operator covers two robot cells.
I would **explain** that AI weld-path planning changes before full hands-on automation.
think: My **setup** skill may be less rare, and my own roster could tighten.
**Hand** welders on short trailer runs may face an even earlier squeeze.
do: **Practise** a new AI weld-path checker only on approved scrap tests with safety sign-off.
**Take** paid supervised supplier training if offered with written current wages and hours.
**Keep** operating the current cell while checking any new roster.
feel: **Anxious** about possible hours loss, though interested in the technology.
S1.quote: I would not leave a good wage for a trial I have merely requested.
fieldNote: **Yusuf** already knows a robot cell, but new path planning still poses a real skill and staffing change.
He would **actually** practise a new AI checker only on approved scrap tests with safety supervision.
The **requested** supplier course becomes training only if a paid supervised place and written wage and hours are offered.

steps.text: Practise new AI weld-path checker only on approved scrap tests with safety sign-off
Take paid supplier course only if offered supervised with current wages and hours
Check posted nearby welding jobs if no course with mortgage-covering pay and school-compatible shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shop that AGI in 2028 can write weld programs, while capable robots that load, inspect and rework frames follow around 2031. Our present arm already welds, but it still needs human hands at the jig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the plant to need far fewer cell operators when robots handle the whole frame around 2031. I have nine months saved, but that does not replace my high wage for years, and my printed clips could face robot competition too. I would be awake thinking about the mortgage and the children’s school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would list the mortgage and my confirmed factory pay, stop buying printer filament for unbooked clip designs, and move part of each newly paid shift into emergency savings. I would apply for posted local robot-maintenance roles only if paid safety instruction is provided and the wage covers our bills. I would keep the present cell until an actual offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about losing most of the factory wage. A nine-month cushion buys a search, but I would still be awake counting how long it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would a maintenance role survive capable robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might only buy time during installation and early faults. I would check the contract length and the posted pay before moving. A short project would not carry our mortgage unless another confirmed wage followed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a robot for the garage now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would only buy one after a customer pays for a safe job it can do, and I have checked space and insurance. I know how quickly an exciting machine becomes an expensive object in the corner.

say: I would **tell** coworkers 2028 program writing differs from around-2031 robot loading and rework.
The **present** welding arm still needs an operator at the trailer jig.
think: I **expect** far fewer cell-operator hours when capable robots handle the full frame.
**Nine** months saved will not replace my higher wage over a long gap.
do: **Stop** buying printer stock for clip designs with no orders.
**Transfer** part of new factory wages into emergency savings.
Apply for **posted local maintenance** with paid safety training and adequate wages; change only with mortgage-covering contract or confirmed follow-on wages.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss, awake counting mortgage months.
S2.quote: A nine-month cushion buys a search, but I would still be awake counting how long it lasts.
fieldNote: **Yusuf** distinguishes the existing robot arm from future capable robots that could load and rework frames.
He **expects** a major wage loss around 2031 and treats his nine-month reserve as a time limit, not a solution.
**Maintenance** is only a bridge if a posted safe role, adequate wage and workable contract exist.

steps.text: Stop buying printer filament for unbooked clip designs
Transfer part of newly paid factory shifts into emergency savings
Apply for posted local robot-maintenance work only with paid safety instruction and bill-covering wage
Accept maintenance work only if contract covers mortgage or another confirmed wage follows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell operators five years is time to learn how to maintain a full cell and test a small business without betting the house. AGI writes paths by 2031, but capable frame-handling robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 51 when those robots reach the jig, I may lose the old operator role. My clip orders give me a customer list, not a replacement wage. I want the factory paying the mortgage while I learn whether a safe repair service can earn its own fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enroll in a certified robotics-maintenance course next year if the fee fits after bills and the evening schedule fits school pickup. I would ask the plant for paid supervised practice on a new cell if offered, then apply for a posted maintenance role only if the wage covers our mortgage. For the side business, I would accept paid repair bookings only after a customer deposit and documented safety checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the old role shrinking, but five years lets me test one repair job at a time. I can keep our reserve while the orders are still small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first repair you would take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A stopped cell with a documented sensor fault, isolated power and a shop willing to supervise access. I would not buy a robot arm just to advertise a repair service. One paid safe job tells me more than ten plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the college course is not recognised by local employers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the welding-cell job and check posted operator vacancies at nearby factories. I would apply only where pay covers the mortgage and the shift fits our children’s pickup. I would not spend the course fee to collect an unrecognised badge.

say: I would **ask** for recognised maintenance training and paid safe cell practice.
The **five-year** gap permits testing demand before capable robots take full frames.
think: My **operator** role may shrink around 2034 at age 51.
A **clip** customer list does not yet provide a mortgage-sized repair wage.
do: **Take** recognised affordable maintenance training with school pickup and paid supervised plant practice if offered.
**Take** deposited repair bookings only after documented power isolation and safety checks.
**Apply** for posted mortgage-covering maintenance work after training; if course unrecognised, seek posted bill-covering operator work with school-compatible shifts.
feel: **Anxious** about losing the old role, with time to test paid repairs.
S3.quote: I would not buy a robot arm just to advertise a repair service.
fieldNote: **Yusuf** is willing to move early but insists on a locally recognised course and safe supervised practice.
His **small** clip business provides contacts, not assured income for robot maintenance.
A **rejected** certificate leads to an independent posted operator search with mortgage and pickup terms.

steps.text: Take recognised affordable maintenance course with pickup and paid supervised plant practice if offered
Take deposited robot repair bookings only after documented isolation and safety checks
Apply for posted maintenance role after course only if wage covers mortgage
Seek posted operator work if course unrecognised and pay covers mortgage and school pickup fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell younger welders that a decade is enough to train and compare wages, if employers actually post the jobs. I would ask for a real apprenticeship rota rather than a robot photograph on the noticeboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when AGI writes paths in 2036 and 56 when capable robots reach full frame work around 2039. I might be in maintenance by then, or still on a cell if the factory keeps people. The mortgage does not become optional because I enjoy new machinery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the welding-cell wage now and take a locally accepted maintenance course if tuition and school pickup fit. I would accept only deposited weekend repair work with safe access, then save part of each new repair payment after materials. In the first year after 2036 I would apply for a posted local maintenance job only if its wage and shifts cover our mortgage; I would not resign before a written offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about where live factory roles end, but our income is sound in the near term. I can test a service before I rent a workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rent a repair unit with ten years to build it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after repeat paid repair jobs cover rent, insurance and our family bills without using the nine-month reserve. A garage bench is enough for small safe work. I would show Hana the numbers before signing a lease.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would let them see how I check a weld and ask how the robot made its decision. I do not want them to think a screen is either magic or a cheat. They can choose their own work when they are older.

say: I would **ask** for posted apprenticeships and real wage terms before factory change.
**Younger** welders should learn how to test a robot’s work, not only press start.
think: At 53 **when** thinking AGI arrives I might still run the welding cell.
At 56 **near** capable robots, maintenance needs a real paid opening to protect the mortgage.
do: **Keep** earning on the current welding cell while checking accepted maintenance training.
**Take** deposited safe repair jobs and save from newly paid work after costs.
**Apply** for posted maintenance work after 2036 only if pay and shift cover our mortgage.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant roles, while current income and savings feel sound.
S4.quote: The mortgage does not become optional because I enjoy new machinery.
fieldNote: **Yusuf’s** technical curiosity stays tied to a good present wage and nine months of household savings.
He **makes** maintenance study depend on local acceptance, tuition and pickup; later applications depend on posted wage and shifts.
**Repair** work requires deposits, safe access and actual net pay before new saving or a workshop lease.

steps.text: Take locally accepted maintenance course only if tuition and school pickup fit
Take deposited weekend robot repairs only with safe access
Save part of new repair payments after materials
Apply for posted maintenance work only if wage and shift cover mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year AGI picture worries me most because capable robots could take most welding-cell hours around 2031 before my repair work is a real wage. A paid safe maintenance route and a posted local role with bill-covering pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the jig before a trailer frame is welded. A robot can lay a perfect seam on a crooked frame, and the customer will still get a crooked trailer.

headlineQuote: A robot can lay a perfect seam on a crooked frame, and the customer will still get a crooked trailer.
portrait: **Yusuf** Kowalski, 43, runs a farm-trailer welding cell and holds a vocational certificate.
He and **partner** Hana have two school-age children, a mortgage, higher operator pay and about nine months of expenses saved.
He **uses** AI daily for manuals, prints motorbike clips on weekends and tests every physical weld or paid repair.
He is **curious** about new tools but requires recognised training, paid safe practice and posted mortgage-covering roles before leaving wages.
**Fast** AGI alarms him because program writing changes in 2028 and capable robots may remove most cell shifts around 2031.
biggestWorry: The 2028 **AGI** scenario may cut most cell hours when capable robots reach full frame work around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** safe maintenance training and a posted local role with mortgage-covering wages would help.
